paragraphs.heading: Push against the walls
paragraphs.text: Blood pressure is the push of circulating blood against the walls of the vessels it flows through. Most of that push comes from the heart pumping blood around the body. Used on its own, the term means the pressure in a brachial artery, which is the usual place to measure it. It generally refers to the pressure in the arteries of the systemic circulation.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the two numbers
paragraphs.text: A reading is written as two numbers: the systolic pressure, the highest point during one heartbeat, over the diastolic pressure, the lowest point between beats. The units are millimetres of mercury (mmHg) or kilopascals (kPa). The gap between the two numbers is called the pulse pressure, and the average over a whole heartbeat cycle is the mean arterial pressure. For a resting adult, the AHA and ACC call normal anything under 120/80 mmHg, the ESC uses under 120/70 mmHg, and normal also means over 90/60 mmHg.

paragraphs.heading: What moves it
paragraphs.text: Cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance, blood volume and how stiff the arteries are all influence blood pressure. It shifts with a person's situation, emotional state, activity and health, and with temperature, noise, stress, food and drink, posture, drugs and disease. Age and sex play a part too. Over short spans of time, baroreceptors regulate it, acting through the brain on the nervous system and the endocrine system.

paragraphs.heading: Too high or too low
paragraphs.text: Pressure that is consistently too high is called hypertension, pressure that is too low is hypotension, and normal pressure is normotension. Long-term hypertension raises the risk of many diseases, including stroke, heart disease and kidney failure. There is no accepted standard for hypotension, though readings under 90/60 are commonly regarded as low, and in practice pressure counts as too low only when it causes symptoms. The risk of cardiovascular disease climbs steadily once systolic pressure rises above 90 mmHg.

paragraphs.heading: A daily rhythm
paragraphs.text: Blood pressure changes from minute to minute and usually follows a 24-hour cycle, highest in the early morning and evening and lowest at night. Losing that normal fall at night is linked with a greater future risk of cardiovascular disease. Since readings vary so much, and readings from an automated device over 24 hours predict outcomes better, some authorities such as NICE in the UK prefer this ambulatory method for diagnosing hypertension.

paragraphs.heading: Changes over a lifetime
paragraphs.text: Children have lower normal ranges than adults, and these depend on their height. In adults in most societies, systolic pressure tends to rise from early adulthood up to at least age 70, while diastolic pressure starts falling earlier, around age 55. Pulse pressure rises markedly after 40, a change put down to the arteries growing stiffer. Even so, this rise with age is not considered healthy, and some isolated communities do not show it at all.
